tagline: Seven emirates of desert and skyline
overview:
The United Arab Emirates sits on the southeastern corner of the Arabian Peninsula, with long coasts on the Persian Gulf and a short one on the Gulf of Oman, bordering Saudi Arabia and Oman. It covers about 83,600 km², a little smaller than Austria, and most of it is desert.

Roughly 10 million people live in the UAE, but only around one in ten is an Emirati citizen; the rest come from India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, the Philippines, Egypt and dozens of other countries to work. Arabic is the official language and English is used almost everywhere. Abu Dhabi is the capital and largest emirate; Dubai is the best-known city.

The country is a federation of seven emirates, each with its own ruler, joined under a president. Oil made it wealthy from the 1960s, and it has since built airlines, ports, finance and tourism, along with some of the tallest buildings in the world.
landAndNature: Sand dunes cover most of the interior, part of the great Rub al Khali, reaching south toward the Liwa oasis where date palms grow in long green strips. The Hajar Mountains rise in the east near Fujairah, bare and jagged, cut by wadis that flood after rare rains. Summers are extremely hot and humid along the coast, often above 45°C, and the country relies on desalinated seawater. Mangroves fringe parts of the coast and shelter flamingos and young fish, and the waters hold dugongs, second in number only to Australia's. The Arabian oryx, once hunted to extinction in the wild, was bred in captivity and returned to reserves here, and the sand gazelle and Arabian leopard survive in small numbers.
peopleAndCulture: Emirati culture keeps desert and sea traditions alive: falconry, which has UNESCO heritage status, camel racing with robot jockeys, and the ayyala dance, performed with rows of men swinging thin canes. Pearling was the old livelihood before oil, and dhow boats still sail the creeks. Coffee with cardamom, dates, machboos spiced rice and luqaimat, sweet fried dough balls in date syrup, are traditional foods, though restaurants serve dishes from all over the world. Most Emiratis are Muslim, and Ramadan reshapes the daily rhythm. Because the population is so international, dozens of languages are heard on a single street. Cricket, soccer and camel racing all draw crowds, and the country hosts Formula One and major tennis and golf tournaments.
history: Trading settlements and copper mines existed here 4,000 years ago, connected to Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley. For centuries, coastal towns lived on pearl diving, fishing and trade with India and East Africa. Britain signed treaties with local rulers in the 1800s, giving the area the name Trucial States, and took charge of their foreign affairs. Japanese cultured pearls ruined the pearl trade in the 1930s, bringing hard years. Oil was discovered in Abu Dhabi in 1958. When Britain withdrew from the Gulf, Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan led the union of six emirates on December 2, 1971, with Ras Al Khaimah joining in 1972. Oil income built schools, hospitals, roads and cities at remarkable speed, turning small coastal towns into global hubs within one lifetime.
funFacts: The Burj Khalifa in Dubai is the world's tallest building at 828 meters, with more than 160 floors.
Dubai International is one of the busiest airports in the world for international passengers.
The UAE sent a spacecraft, Hope, into orbit around Mars in 2021, the first Arab interplanetary mission.
Emirati falcons travel with their own passports and can sit in aircraft cabins on certain airlines.
The Liwa oasis grows millions of date palms, and one Emirati date festival awards prizes for the finest fruit.
